messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For as long as he could remember, Robert had taken pride in his ability to think clearly. At seventy-two, still working as a software engineer, he valued precision, logic, and control. That was what made the years of captivity so unbearable—not just the physical pain, but the way his own mind had been turned against him. The interrogators had not only broken his body; they had made him complicit in his own undoing. They had forced him, under threat of worse, to sign statements he knew were lies, to read aloud confessions that vilified people he loved. Robert had never spoken of this to anyone. He had tried hard not to think about it at all.

But the thoughts would not stay buried. When they surfaced—a flash of a cold concrete room, the sound of a door bolting shut—he would push them down with all his strength, sometimes physically shaking his head as if to dislodge the images. He had come to believe that if he let himself dwell on those memories, even for a moment, he might lose his grip entirely. He monitored his own thoughts constantly, scanning for any sign that he was slipping, that the man who had been broken in that room was still there, waiting to take over. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but what the memory proved: that he had acted in ways that went against everything he believed he was. He had betrayed his own values to survive, and that fact had hollowed him out from the inside.

In the years since, Robert had lost his faith in people entirely. He lived alone in a small house with a deadbolt on every door and a chain lock he checked three times before bed. Even so, he had difficulty falling asleep. He would lie awake in the dark, ears straining, certain that staying alert was the only thing keeping him safe. He had come to see danger in the smallest cues—a neighbor’s prolonged glance, a stranger’s posture on the bus. He studied faces and body language obsessively, searching for signs of threat. A man standing too still in a grocery aisle could ruin his entire afternoon; he would leave without buying anything, heart pounding, convinced he had narrowly avoided something terrible.

His work kept him indoors, which suited him. He wrote code from home, communicating with colleagues only through email and chat. But his house had become a cage of its own. He could not stand being alone in a room for more than a few minutes; he would leave doors open, move from room to room, keep the television on for the sound of human voices. Yet when he was around actual people, he felt isolated and set apart from them. They seemed to move through life without the weight he carried. He was certain that if they knew what he had done—what he had been forced to do—they would see him as he saw himself: a man who had failed the most basic test of character.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. He had not seen his brother in nearly a decade, turning down every invitation with vague excuses about work. He had stopped attending the community center where he used to play chess. His world had shrunk to the dimensions of his home office and the short path to his mailbox. What finally brought Robert to seek help was not a crisis, but a slow recognition that he was running out of room to hide. A new colleague had been assigned to his team—a young woman with a direct, confident gaze—and he found himself unable to look at her face without scanning for threat. He had begun checking his locks three times before sitting down to work, then again at lunch, then again before bed. He was exhausted. He was afraid that the man in the concrete room had never really left, and that the only way forward was to face what he had spent decades trying not to see.
